rv.q: Alex Rugman’s debut play about sibling rivalry on a dystopian space mission struggles to marry its themes
The Urmetazoan is a small story of cosmic value.
This is an intelligent debut by Rugman.
Overall, a story that was riveting in parts and lukewarm in others.
There is merit and considerable potential but facts and characters require far greater integration to fully convince beyond a novice’s level.
Yet the evening is underwhelming, lacking in urgency.
The Urmetazoan ultimately becomes less about whether humanity can survive on another planet and more about what we carry with us when we leave someone behind.
Overall, Rugman’s debut play is sharp, compelling and thought-provoking, even if its ambition is occasionally constrained by repetition.
Unfortunately, the script places certain limitations on the development of the sisters' relationship.
Those who can push through will be rewarded with a brilliant production from start to finish.

Propelled by a standout leading performance from Myer-Bennett, The Urmetazoan promises a journey for both sisters, one where they will boldly go where they have not before, and one that is both devastating and deeply profound for its audience.
Myer-Bennett and Treadway are so natural in their exceptional performances you could mistake them for actual sisters.
What has evolved is a very human story about letting go.
While Rugman’s central premise is an interesting one, the narrative’s shifting focus and repetition mean that it never decides what it wants to be, hampering its dramatic impact.

cn.t: Rugman's debut about estranged sisters reuniting before one leaves for Mars earns praise for its tender performances and intimate approach to big ideas, though some critics find the space travel elements more compelling than the family drama.
